author: A. Stein
asr_identification: Bannu district
evidence: Passing through Bannu on the 1926-27 tour, Stein refers back to his 1904-05 report for the Chinese pilgrims' accounts of Bannu: Fa-hsien's Po-na and Hsüan-tsang's Fa-la-na.
quote: the descriptions left by the Chinese pilgrims of … the fertile and always important district of Bannu
note: Stein restates the Bannu = 伐剌拏 identification; the basis is his 1904-05 report (pp. 5 sq.), following Cunningham. No new evidence.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: small stupa near Idak, c. 27 miles from Bannu
evidence: At Ark-ghundai, a fortified hillock in the Tochi valley about 27 miles from Bannu, Stein finds a massive enclosing wall and a solid circular mass he takes to be a small stupa. A copper coin of Kanishka from the hillock (other Kushan coins reported) dates the occupation to Buddhist times.
quote: Remains of ruined Stupa … I belieA'e, it may safely be taken to . mark . the remains a small … Site occupied in Buddhist times. — The dating of the occupation of the … site from Buddhist times is confirmed by a copper coin of Kaniska
note: Buddhist remains on Mizutani's/Stein's Bannu (北) side of the route, but dated by Kushan coins, not to the 7th century.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: possible Buddhist cult spot
evidence: A long, low stone platform near Spin with no local tradition attached; Stein conjectures that, like the 'giant's graves' of the Peshawar valley, it may mark a former Buddhist cult object (a nirvana image).
quote: symbolic representation of Buddha ih'^i^ana had once enjoyed local worship
note: Speculative only; Stein dates nothing. Weak support for Buddhism in Waziristan.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: ruined site with probable small stupas
evidence: At Khore-narai, north of his camp in the Spin area, a dug-up circular foundation c. 18 ft across, 'likely to have been a Stupa', and a small undisturbed circular stone mound that 'might also' be one; reported 'inscriptions' proved to be mere graffiti.
quote: measming about IS feet in diameter and likely to liave … might also, mark the - remains of a Stupa
note: Possible Buddhist remains in southern Waziristan; undated.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: Waziristan, perhaps with adjacent hill tracts south of the Gumal
evidence: Stein quotes Xuanzang's note on the country west of Fa-la-na (separate chiefs and no supreme ruler, sheep and fine horses). He holds that the description and position 'leave no doubt' Waziristan is meant, repeating his 1904-05 discussion; the Wazir and Baluch horse breeds he takes to be indigenous.
quote: Locatioii of Hsuan-tsang’s Ki-kiang-na … the hill region now known as AA^a&istan is meant, together pSrliaps ,witli some … the Chinese pilgrim’s account represents the conditions prevailing domi to our
note: This is Stein's explicit identification, which Mizutani follows. Its basis is the description (tribal chiefs, horses), the westward position from Bannu and, for him, the Arab Qiqan (S006), not any find.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: Waziristan
evidence: Stein matches the Arab Qiqan, said to lie north of Sind near Arokhaj, with Ki-kiang-na by name. Baladhuri's account of al-Muhallab's raid in AH 44 (AD 664-5) names 'Banna and al-Ahwar, between Multan and Kabul' and a defeat of Turkish horsemen in Qiqan; Stein takes this to confirm Qiqan = Waziristan, and the fine horses agree with Xuanzang.
quote: Arab historians’ mention of Qiqan … coimects Qiqan with -Baimh … suffices tbVi, colffirm the identification of Qiqan m'th Waziristan
note: Stein's Qiqan rests on Baladhuri linking it with Banna (Bannu). Stein notes (p. 30 n. 4) that other passages (Baladhuri, Muqaddasi) tie Qiqan to Sind, Sibi and Khorasan. The Baluchistan gazetteers' Kikan at Nal is not discussed.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: Bannu (Marquart had earlier proposed Gandawa)
evidence: In a footnote Stein says Marquart now accepts Banna = Bannu, but in Eransahr p. 276 he had been inclined to look for Banna, i.e. Fa-la-na, at Gandawa in Sind (Kachhi).
quote: he was inclined to look for Banna;. Fada-na in Gandawa, Sind.
note: An early southern placement of 伐剌拏 at Gandava (Marquart 1901), which Mirchandani's route uses for 11.22 instead; Marquart later withdrew it.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: Arachosia and Zabulistan of the Arabs, capital Ghazni
evidence: Stein explains why the Arabs called the people of Qiqan 'Turks': the T'ang Annals show that the great territory of Ts'ao-chu-ch'a (Arokhaj/Zabulistan, capital Ghazni, on Waziristan's western border) was then largely of Turkish stock.
quote: great territory of Ts‘ao-chu.-ch‘a, corresponduig … Ghazni, on the western- .borders of Waziristan
note: Stein accepts 漕矩吒 = Zabulistan/Arachosia with its capital at Ghazni. That puts Waziristan as the neighbour of 漕矩吒 on its east, which fits the Bannu–Waziristan route.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: burial cairns of the early centuries AD
evidence: Burial cairns at Moghul-ghundai in Zhob; an intaglio ring suggests Kushan or Gupta work and the deposits are no older than the early centuries AD. Stein compares their pottery with that of Tor-dherai and 'other Buddhist sites'.
quote: made by me at Tor-dlierai” and other Buddhist sites I had occasion to examine
note: Early-historical Zhob; nothing Buddhist in itself, nothing on Opokien.

author: A. Stein
name_in_asr: Dabar-kot mound, Thal plain (Duki area, Loralai)
asr_identification: late occupation including the Sasanian period
evidence: In area D.E.ii of the great Dabar-kot mound in the Thal plain below Duki, Stein finds a homestead with a thin silver coin 'safely' recognised as Sasanian, and a relief-decorated sherd with a Sasanian-looking motif: occupation in the historical period, after the chalcolithic layers.
quote: a thin silver coin which, though much corroded … can be safely recognized as belonging to a Sasanian issue
note: This is the one find of Xuanzang's general period in the Duki area, Mirchandani's capital region for 伐剌拏. It shows occupation, not a city or Buddhism.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: Buddhist stupa site with inscriptions
evidence: The contents list a section 'The Buddhist remains of Tor-dherai' and an appendix on the Tor-dherai inscriptions. The OCR breaks off at the beginning of the stupa description (base with pilasters, the stupa proper on the hill-top, Stein camped at Dabar-kot), so the inscriptions and dating are not in this text.
quote: iii. The Buddhist remains of Tor-dherai … my camp stood at Dnbar-kot … Stupa proper. On theX south
note: The Tor-dherai stupa (AR 1926-27: Kushan, Kharoshthi and Brahmi sherds) lies in the Thal–Duki plain on Mirchandani's route for 11.23. Its date is Kushan per AR; the OCR here is incomplete.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: Arab base for the invasion of India
evidence: Stein notes the dread of barren Makran in the reports of the Arab commanders who, under the early Caliphs, tried to use Makran as a base for the invasion of India.
quote: the early Caliphs orders endeavoured to use hlakran as a base for the mvasion
note: General 7th-century context for Makran; no place names, no Xuanzang.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: chief centre of population of Makran since early times
evidence: Stein describes the Turbat oasis on the Kej river as probably the chief centre of population in Makran since early times, whence the mediaeval name Kej Makran for the whole country; the Kej valley is the natural highway through the country.
quote: This oasis appears to have … formed an important if not tin, chief centie of population m
note: Supports Kech (the Arab Kiz) as Makran's main centre, on the Kech-valley road west to Persian Makran (Mirchandani's route to Kasarkand). He gives no 7th-century or Buddhist evidence.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: castle on an ancient debris mound
evidence: The Miri castle at Turbat, built up by successive rulers of Makran to about 120 ft, stands on an ancient debris mound; the fragments are prehistoric painted pottery and later glazed ware. Stein made no trial excavation.
quote: It has been bmlt up by the efforts ot succes … Fragments of rrehistone pottery
note: Continuous occupation of the Kech capital site, but there is no datable pre-Islamic historical layer and nothing Buddhist.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: Arab-period centre; named in 7th-century Arab enterprises against Sind
evidence: Stein says the earliest historical notices for Jhalawan concern Khozdar, repeatedly mentioned in connection with the Arab enterprises of the 7th century against Sind, owing to its position at a meeting of routes from Makran, Sind, Kandahar and the coast.
quote: lelite to Khozdar which t? repcatedlj mentioned … m oonne\ion w ith Aiah enterprises m the sevnitli centuij agamst Snid
note: Khozdar was a known centre in the 7th century (Mirchandani's capital for 臂多勢羅), but on textual grounds only.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: small sites; early Muhammadan tombs, mediaeval glazed ware
evidence: At Khozdar there are no large mounds. Miri but, the best-known site, has domed Muhammadan tombs on hillocks sacred 'in early Muhammadan times', polychrome mediaeval glazed ware, a brick kiln, and no prehistoric pottery.
quote: the absence of any large … sanctity m early Muhammadan times and hence been chosen as bunal grounds
note: Confirms the gazetteers (B037) and Hargreaves: Khozdar's remains are Islamic, with nothing pre-Arab or Buddhist.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: Kalima, 4th-5th century AH (per Denison Ross)
evidence: About 9 miles from Khozdar on the road to Baghwana, a rock inscription in Kufic letters contains the Kalima. It is identical with the one in the Gazetteer that Denison Ross dated to the 4th or 5th century AH.
quote: It proved to contain tie Kaima the Muhammadan confession of faith
note: Islamic period only.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: pass with ancient Gabar-band dams and a barrage; no town
evidence: North of the Lakorian pass Stein crosses a succession of massive Gabar-bands. Half a mile south of the Lakorian–Anjira watershed is a large stone barrage, 348 yards long, built to store water for irrigation. He describes dams and terraces only, no ruined city.
quote: Gabjr bands north of Likorjjn pass … unmistakably ancient barrage which is met four miles further on … the watershed between the valle)s of Lakorian
note: This is the ground behind Cunningham/Mizutani's 'great ruined city of Lakorian'. Stein finds irrigation works only, no city, so Lākoriān as the capital of 狼揭羅 is weakened further. The Gabar-bands are undated.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: taken by an earlier traveller for defences
evidence: A footnote (badly OCR'd) cites an earlier 'Journey to Kalat', apparently Masson's, which notes the Gabar-bands of Lakorian as remarkable among the antiquities of Jhalawan and assumes them to have been places of defence. Stein shows they are irrigation dams.
quote: Ho assumes (.hem to have bein plpcts of ddenca
note: This probably explains the 'ruined city' that reached Cunningham: dams misread as fortifications. Further against Lākoriān as 窣菟黎濕伐羅.

author: A. Stein
asr_identification: mound with ribbed pottery
evidence: The pottery at Surkh damb has ribbed decoration like that of NW Frontier sites of Buddhist times. A ceramic analogy only; there is no glazed ware.
quote: sites of the N W Piontier dating from Buddhist times
note: Not evidence of Buddhism in Jhalawan.
